raw_case_text:
An 81-year-old woman with recently diagnosed uncontrolled diabetes presented to the emergency department with rapidly progressive mental status change. Two months prior, she was admitted for diabetic ketoacidosis, found to have an A1C of 14.7%, and ultimately discharged on insulin. Over the following month, she experienced progressive cognitive decline. At baseline, she was able to carry out activities of daily living (ADLs) and then over the course of a month, she declined to the point that she was only responsive to name and minimally arousable. Relevant medications included recent prescriptions of memantine and sertraline for which the patient's sister endorsed no missed doses. The history was obtained from the sister who stated the patient had no acute complaints prior to these symptoms. Upon initial examination, she was noted to be hemodynamically stable and only minimally arousable to speech. Brudzinski's and Kernig's signs were negative and hyperreflexia was evident on her patellar reflex. An initial extensive serological evaluation was unremarkable (Table 1). Brain imaging was obtained with computed tomography and subsequently magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure 1), which demonstrated microvascular changes consistent with age without acute intracranial pathology
Electroencephalogram (EEG) demonstrated decreased generalized activity but otherwise unremarkable. A lumbar puncture (LP) was performed with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showing lymphocyte pleocytosis, low glucose, and elevated protein (Table 2), raising suspicion for infectious meningitis and prompting initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics, antiviral drugs, and corticosteroids. HIV screening was negative. On the third hospital day, cryptococcal antigen from the LP returned positive as did the India ink stain. Prior antimicrobials were discontinued and amphotericin 4 mg/kg every 24 h was initiated. Flucytosine was not available, so fluconazole (renal dosing) 400 mg PO once daily was used as an alternative. Two-week follow-up CSF cultures were without growth, and she was transitioned to fluconazole consolidation. Atovaquone was also started for opportunistic prophylaxis in the setting of identified lymphopenia. Over the next few months, the patient slowly returned to baseline and was able to perform all ADLs/instrumental ADLs. Following discharge, she was evaluated as an outpatient for lymphopenia that was noted while inpatient. Upon further review of labs, she was noted to have lymphocytopenia for over 10 years although a CD4 count had never been obtained. CD4 count was noted to be decreased at 79 cells/microl, HIV remained negative, and an autoimmune workup was initiated (Table 3). She was subsequently found to have elevated antinuclear antibody (ANA) dilution of 1:640 and anti-double-stranded DNA level of 70 IU/ml. These serologic findings in the setting of leukopenia without alternative cause led to the diagnosis of SLE. Idiopathic CD4 + lymphopenia was entertained, but the constellation of the patient's symptoms coupled with the strong positive ANA and elevated anti-dsDNA level favored a diagnosis of SLE. Mild proteinuria was also noted on urologic assessment. She was started on hydroxychloroquine and remained stable at subsequent follow-ups.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 81-year-old woman with recently diagnosed uncontrolled diabetes mellitus presented with a 1-month history of rapidly progressive cognitive decline and obtundation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two months prior to presentation, the patient had been hospitalized for diabetic ketoacidosis (HbA1c 14.7%) and discharged on insulin. Over the subsequent month, despite full adherence to her medications (including memantine and sertraline), she declined from independent baseline functioning to being minimally arousable and responsive only to her name.
subjective.past_medical_history: Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus diagnosed 2 months prior during an admission for diabetic ketoacidosis (HbA1c 14.7%); 10-year history of uninvestigated chronic lymphocytopenia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for rapidly progressive cognitive decline and obtundation. Home medications: insulin, memantine, and sertraline.

objective.physical_examination: Hemodynamically stable, minimally arousable to speech (responsive only to name), negative Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs, and patellar hyperreflexia.
objective.routine_investigations: Chronic lymphocytopenia, negative HIV screening, mild proteinuria, and subsequent outpatient autoimmune workup showing positive ANA (titer 1:640) and elevated anti-dsDNA antibody (70 IU/mL).
objective.advanced_workup: Head CT and brain MRI showed age-related microvascular changes without acute intracranial pathology; EEG showed generalized background slowing. Lumbar puncture CSF revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, elevated protein, and (on hospital day 3) positive CSF cryptococcal antigen and positive CSF India ink stain. Outpatient immunological evaluation revealed a low CD4+ T-cell count of 79 cells/uL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis presenting as rapidly progressive dementia/obtundation and unmasking late-onset systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with severe CD4+ lymphopenia (CD4 79 cells/uL), confirmed by positive CSF cryptococcal antigen and India ink stain alongside ANA 1:640, anti-dsDNA 70 IU/mL, leukopenia/lymphopenia, and proteinuria. Empirical antibacterials/antivirals were stopped on day 3 and she was treated with IV amphotericin B (4 mg/kg every 24 hours) plus renally dosed oral fluconazole (400 mg daily, as flucytosine was unavailable), achieving negative CSF cultures at 2 weeks, transition to fluconazole consolidation and atovaquone prophylaxis, full recovery of baseline ADLs over several months, and stabilization on hydroxychloroquine.
